payload.source_label: Equation (1.1) is a conservation law with linear flux f(q) = A q

contract.statement: The constant-coefficient real linear system q_t + A q_x = 0 for an m-component field in one space dimension is a conservation law q_t + ∂_x(f(q)) = 0 with flux f(v) = Av (printed page 1, equation (1.1); printed page 3, equation (1.8); printed page 4, opening sentence). Constancy and linearity explain the agreement of the spatial terms. The selected passage states this identification without an exact regularity class; the surrounding source treats smoothness and discontinuous solutions separately (printed page 4, Section 1.1.2).
assumptions: The referenced problem has the homogeneous constant-coefficient form q_t(x,t) + A q_x(x,t) = 0 in one space dimension (printed page 1, equation (1.1) and preceding sentence).
A is constant and real, with dimensions matching the m-component field (printed page 1, paragraph following equation (1.1)).

The differential equations are understood where the displayed partial derivatives exist; this is inherited differential-form context, not an explicitly quantified regularity hypothesis in the selected sentence (printed pages 1 and 3, equations (1.1) and (1.8); printed page 4, Section 1.1.2 smoothness qualification).
The chapter studies time-dependent, homogeneous first-order systems with one spatial variable in the displayed formulation (printed page 1, introduction to equation (1.1)).

The surrounding section concerns hyperbolic conservation laws. The selected identification as a conservation law does not expressly impose an additional spectral hypothesis; distinguishing its algebraic content from the chapter's hyperbolic setting is an analyst interpretation supported by the separate hyperbolicity definition and the unqualified identification sentence (printed page 3, opening discussion and Section 1.1; printed page 4, opening sentence).

The source distinguishes the differential formulation from an integral formulation and discusses discontinuous solutions separately; the selected sentence itself does not formulate a weak-solution claim (printed page 4, Sections 1.1.1–1.1.2).
quantifiers: x and t are real spatial and temporal variables; q : R × R → R^m is the unknown field (printed page 1, equation (1.1) and its explanatory paragraph).
m is the number of components of q, and A is a constant m × m real matrix (printed page 1, paragraph following equation (1.1)).

The flux is f(v) = Av for a state v in R^m; v is analyst notation distinguishing the flux argument from the field q(x,t) (printed pages 3–4, sentence identifying the linear flux, together with equation (1.8)).
